items.title: Biologie clinique | Pr Manel Chaabane élue présidente de la FIFBCML
items.description: Dix-neuf ans après sa création à Hammamet, la Fédération internationale francophone de biologie clinique et de médecine de laboratoire (FIFBCML) a élu à les Tunisiennes Pr Manel Chaabane, comme présidente, et Pr Yosr Galai comme secrétaire générale adjointe, toutes deux pour la Société tunisienne de biologie clinique (STBC). Dr Khalil Ben Abdallah, président du Syndicat tunisien des biologistes privés (STBP), a été élu représentant des membres affiliés. La FIFBCML réunit les sociétés et syndicats de biologie médicale de l’espace francophone. Elle a été fondée le 11 mai 2007 à Hammamet par cinq pays : l’Algérie, la France, le Liban, le Maroc et la Tunisie. Elle compte aujourd’hui 17 sociétés savantes issues de 9 pays, sur 3 continents. En 2027, avec l’arrivée de l’Association des médecins biochimistes du Québec et de la Société Burkinabé de biologie clinique, elle réunira 19 membres de 11 pays, sur 4 continents. Son objectif est de faire de la francophonie un canal d’échange entre les professionnels de la biologie clinique, au service de la formation, de la qualité des analyses et de la santé publique. La Tunisie, pays fondateur, occupera ainsi trois sièges au bureau de la fédération. C’est une reconnaissance de la place de la biologie médicale tunisienne dans l’espace francophone, et du travail mené ensemble par ses biologistes du secteur public, avec la STBC, et du secteur privé, avec le STBP. Cette nouvelle présidence sera à l’honneur lors du 4 e Congrès national de biologie médicale (CNBM 2026), organisé par le STBP les 6 et 7 novembre 2026 à l’hôtel Oceana de Hammamet. Placé sous les auspices de la FIFBCML, le congrès réunira plus de 300 biologistes, des délégations d’Algérie, du Maroc et de France, ainsi que des représentants de la FIFBCML. Le vendredi 6 novembre, une table ronde inter-syndicale de la FIFBCML, «Biologie médicale 2030 : nouvelles formes d'exercice, nouvelles missions» , précédera l’assemblée générale de la fédération. Le 2 e Forum tunisien de biologie médicale, prévu les 28, 29 et 30 avril 2027, sera le premier rendez-vous de la nouvelle présidence. Coorganisé par la STBC, le STBP et la FIFBCML, il réunira les biologistes tunisiens et francophones des secteurs public et privé. Dr Khalil Ben Abdallah, Président du STBP, représentant des membres affiliés de la FIFBCML, a déclaré : « Voir la Tunisie présider la FIFBCML est un honneur pour tous nos biologistes, du public comme du privé. Aux côtés de Pr Manel Chaabane et de Pr Yosr Galai, nous voulons faire de cette présidence un temps d'ouverture : renforcer la formation et la qualité, porter ensemble les nouvelles missions du biologiste, et donner aux jeunes biologistes francophones une place réelle dans nos travaux.» L’article Biologie clinique | Pr Manel Chaabane élue présidente de la FIFBCML est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Lahore court grants NCCIA further two-day remand of suspects over US postage stamp fraud
items.description: LAHORE: A judicial magistrate on Tuesday granted the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) a further two-day physical remand of two suspects in a Rs35 billion fraud involving the online sale of counterfeit US postage stamps. The prime suspect, identified as a 33-year-old resident of Khanewal, had been charged by a Florida jury with defrauding the United States Postal Service (USPS) of $126 million, the US Attorney’s Office of the Southern District of Florida said on Sept 28. The Lahore NCCIA announced the prime suspect’s arrest in late October, and he was sent on a five-day physical remand on Oct 21. Today’s extension of the physical remand is the third for him, and second for the co-suspect . On Tuesday, the NCCIA produced both men before Judicial Magistrate Naeem Wattoo upon the expiry of their latest four-day remand . The investigating officer (IO) sought custody of the suspects for another five days for interrogation. However, Magistrate Wattoo granted the agency two more days of physical custody and directed the IO to produce the suspects again on Nov 5. According to NCCIA, the initial investigation revealed that the prime suspect operated a website to market and sell over 5m fake US postage stamps over a period of more than three years. According to the US Department of Justice, the website run by the Pakistani national was not authorised to sell USPS products and services. The counterfeit labels allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates “far below legitimate USPS prices”, it said, adding that it caused losses exceeding $126m to the postal service. US prosecutors alleged that the website sold the labels for around $2 each, regardless of a package’s weight, size or destination. A US court order authorised the seizure and shutdown of the website. Money trail In a press conference on Oct 20, NCCIA’s Lahore Zone Additional Director Atif Ameer said that 16 bank accounts had been used in the scam. Seven of the accounts were operated by the suspect, five by his brother, two by his wife, and one each by his sister and aunt. He said the agency had expanded the investigation across several parts of the country. “Eight special teams were formed in Punjab, Islamabad and Sindh to trace the suspect and investigate the network,” he said and added the teams conducted raids at 35 locations and questioned 47 people as part of the investigation. “Investigators also employed digital and forensic techniques to establish the suspect’s movements and identify people associated with the operation.” Ameer added that investigators analysed 122 call-data records, 50 IMEI-tracking reports and audio and video recordings from 120 cameras. “Artificial intelligence and other modern technological tools were also used during the investigation. A locator operation continued for 10 days as investigators attempted to establish the suspect’s whereabouts and trace his activities,” he said. The NCCIA said the major focus of the investigation was the financial trail generated by the online sale of the counterfeit stamps. “We are examining transactions conducted through the 16 bank accounts and attempting to determine the flow of funds between the accounts allegedly belonging to the suspect and his relatives. “The involvement of family members is also being examined as part of the investigation, particularly the alleged use of their bank accounts in connection with the online business,” the additional director said. He said the role of other individuals in operating the website, processing orders, receiving payments or distributing the counterfeit stamps was also being probed. “Investigators are also working to establish the full scale of the operation and verify the volume and value of the transactions,” he said.

items.title: Okala : 2,58 milliards de FCFA pour indemniser 69 propriétaires impactés par les travaux routiers
items.description: Le gouvernement gabonais a bouclé l’opération d’indemnisation des propriétaires dont les biens sont affectés par le prolongement de la route de contournement de l’aéroport, dans le secteur d’Okala. Au total, 2,58 milliards de FCFA ont été mobilisés pour dédommager 69 bénéficiaires, qui recevront également des parcelles avec titres fonciers. La gouverneure de l’Estuaire, Marie-Françoise Dikoumba et le ministre Mays Mouissi lors de la remise des chèques aux bénéficiaires, le 2 novembre 2026. © D.R. Le processus d’indemnisation des populations impactées par les travaux de prolongement de la route de contournement de l’aéroport, dans le secteur d’Okala, est arrivé à son terme. Le lundi 2 novembre 2026, au gouvernorat de l’Estuaire, le ministre du Logement, de l’Habitat, de l’Urbanisme et du Cadastre, Mays Mouissi, a procédé à la remise des derniers chèques aux propriétaires concernés, marquant ainsi la clôture de cette opération. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de la ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Jacqueline Ilogu Bignoumba, et de la gouverneure de l’Estuaire, Marie-Françoise Dikoumba. Cette dernière étape faisait suite à une première distribution organisée le 29 octobre dernier. Au terme du processus, 69 biens situés dans l’emprise du projet ont été recensés et leurs propriétaires indemnisés, pour une enveloppe globale de 2 580 918 867 FCFA. Une vue des bénéficiaires dans la salle. © D.R. Les montants attribués varient selon la nature et la valeur des biens concernés. Le plus important dédommagement versé à un bénéficiaire s’élève ainsi à 640,8 millions de FCFA. Une compensation financière à laquelle s’ajoute une mesure d’accompagnement foncier : les personnes concernées bénéficieront également de parcelles assorties de titres fonciers. Le site destiné à leur relogement a déjà été identifié et son aménagement devrait démarrer dans les prochaines semaines. Au-delà du règlement des indemnisations, cette opération constitue une étape importante dans la mise en œuvre du projet routier d’Okala. Pour les autorités, l’enjeu est désormais de concilier l’avancement des travaux d’infrastructures avec la prise en compte des droits et des préoccupations des populations affectées. Reste à concrétiser, dans les délais annoncés, l’aménagement du site d’accueil et la mise à disposition effective des parcelles promises. items.title: Diplomatie : le Guinéen Siaka Cissoko nommé représentant résident de la CEDEAO au Bénin
items.description: L’ambassadeur guinéen Siaka Cissoko a été nommé représentant résident de la Communauté économique des États de l’Afrique de l’Ouest (CEDEAO) au Bénin. Cette nomination vient consacrer le parcours d’un diplomate chevronné, qui dispose d’une longue expérience dans les domaines de la coopération internationale et de l’intégration africaine. Cette désignation constitue également une nouvelle responsabilité pour ce diplomate, qui a occupé plusieurs fonctions stratégiques au sein de l’administration guinéenne et des mécanismes communautaires de la CEDEAO. Un parcours académique et professionnel diversifié Juriste et économiste du développement, Siaka Cissoko dispose d’une formation pluridisciplinaire acquise notamment en Guinée, en Belgique, aux Pays-Bas, en Chine et au Canada. Titulaire d’un diplôme d’études supérieures en droit public de l’Université de Conakry, il a obtenu un master en gestion et administration publiques à l’Université d’Anvers, en Belgique. Il a également suivi des formations dans les domaines du droit international, de l’économie, de la diplomatie et de la coopération au développement. Une expérience significative dans les institutions guinéennes et communautaires Au cours de sa carrière, il a notamment occupé les fonctions de directeur général de la Coordination des aides extérieures et de directeur général de l’Intégration africaine, ainsi que celle de chef du Bureau national de la CEDEAO au ministère de la Coopération internationale. Son expérience au sein des mécanismes communautaires est également notable. Il a présidé ou participé à plusieurs comités et programmes de la CEDEAO, notamment dans les domaines de la coordination des politiques macroéconomiques, de la libéralisation des échanges commerciaux, du volontariat, des bourses d'excellence, de la promotion des femmes et de la gestion des questions migratoires. Il a par ailleurs pris part à des travaux nationaux sur le tarif extérieur commun de la CEDEAO et l’harmonisation de la balance des paiements. Une nouvelle responsabilité après son passage au Nigeria Avant cette nomination, Siaka Cissoko occupait, jusqu’en mars dernier, les fonctions d’ambassadeur extraordinaire et plénipotentiaire de la République de Guinée auprès du Nigeria, du Tchad et du Bénin, ainsi que de représentant permanent auprès de la CEDEAO. Sa nouvelle mission consistera notamment à contribuer au renforcement des relations entre l’organisation communautaire et le Bénin, dans un contexte ouest-africain marqué par des enjeux de stabilité politique, de sécurité, de mobilité et d’intégration économique. Cette nomination constitue une nouvelle marque de confiance envers ce diplomate guinéen, appelé à mettre son expérience au service de l’organisation sous-régionale. items.title: Latinos Are Still Swing Voters
items.description: Latinos swung further toward Republicans than any other group in 2024, and they could swing further in the opposite direction this year. If Democrats recover the ground they have lost with this bloc over the past decade, it won’t mean that Latinos have come back to their natural political home. We don’t have one. Like many Latinos, I’ve grown tired of having to talk every cycle about whether we lean Democrat or Republican. Are Latinos Democrats, because we support immigrants and workers’ rights? Are we Republicans, because our faith leads us to embrace traditional family values? I expected Donald Trump’s historic success among Latinos in 2024 to prompt fresh thinking about who Latinos are as a community—to foster a deeper understanding of what it means to be Latino, contradictions and all. In 2024, virtually every segment of the Latino population moved to the right—women and men, Catholics and evangelical Protestants, rich and poor, white and nonwhite, in cities and rural areas, the recently naturalized and longtime citizens. Trump energized new Latino voters who hadn’t participated in politics before, and although he may have been the main attraction, other Republicans also did better with Latinos than they had in previous elections. The elections of 2022 and 2024 brought many new Latino faces to Congress, and they came from all over the map. In addition to Latino representatives from Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, New Mexico, and Texas, we had others from New Jersey, Ohio, Oregon, and Washington. They were men and women, Democrats and Republicans. They were mechanics, organizers, business owners, veterans. They had varied interests and didn’t speak with one voice. They were a demonstration of how Latinos were as integrated into American politics as any other group. But two years later, many political observers still see Latinos as one-dimensional actors: as immigrants themselves, or as people instinctively inclined to sympathize with immigrants, or as traitors who are turning our backs to them. The focus on immigration makes sense, up to a point. The border is more secure today than it was under Joe Biden, but instead of dangerous criminals, the targets of ICE arrests have overwhelmingly been law-abiding, if undocumented, immigrants. [ Nick Miroff: Losing the ‘big-ass truck’ vote ] Yet even though Latinos as a group seem likely to vote against Republicans as a reaction against Trump’s immigration and economic policies, Democrats haven’t yet come to a consensus on exactly what immigration and economic policies we will be voting for . In terms of immigration, is it legalization? The end of private detention facilities? The continued deportation of dangerous criminals, but not law-abiding immigrants—à la Barack Obama, whom the left maligned as the deporter in chief? In terms of the economy, is it universal health care? A raised minimum wage? Programs to help Latinos start businesses? Taxing billionaires? The lesson that Democrats seem to have drawn from 2024 is that immigration isn’t a winning issue for them, so they’d better focus on inflation and the cost of living instead. Republicans, meanwhile, want to believe that Latinos care about the economy above all else, because that would give them cover to do whatever they want on immigration. That did seem to be the lesson of 2020 and 2024, when Trump did better and better among Latinos despite his draconian support for mass deportation. Most Latinos favor comprehensive immigration reform and think it’s wrong to deport immigrants who don’t have a criminal record and who have bought homes, raised families, and otherwise integrated into their communities. As the political scientist Matt Barreto told me before the 2024 election, Latinos want the border to be secure, but also think law-abiding immigrants who are longtime residents should be able to legalize. A comprehensive policy based on this distinction is tricky, though, because it leaves unresolved the question of what to do with recent unauthorized arrivals who are both hardworking and law-abiding, which is to say most of them. Since the mass deportations of Trump’s second administration began, we’ve upheld veterans and their families, or immigrants who arrived decades ago and have built a life here, as sympathetic characters unjustly caught up in Trump’s immigration dragnet. But does this mean we should be deporting hardworking immigrants who arrived more recently? Immigrants who came decades ago were new arrivals once, and new arrivals today will one day be immigrants who have been here for a long time. A poll in September, from NBC and Telemundo, showed significant divides within the Latino community on these and other questions. I was surprised to learn how minimally Latinos’ views of immigration have changed over the past few years—even after the arrests, deportations, and killings. When it came to “dealing with immigration,” respondents, by a margin of 45 to 31 percent, said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans. In 2022, that margin was 41 percent to 30 percent in favor of Democrats—that is, only a slightly higher percentage of Hispanics today think Democrats would handle immigration better. [ From the March 2022 Issue: There’s no such thing as ‘the Latino vote’ ] Thirty-eight percent of Latinos believe that Democrats would more effectively secure the border, while an equal percentage believe the reverse. Four years ago, Democrats had an 11-point advantage on that question. Moreover, a lower percentage of Latinos today think immigration “helps more than hurts,” and a higher percentage thinks immigration “hurts more than helps.” Finally, compared with four years ago, a lower percentage of Latinos think that immigrants brought to the United States when they were kids should be legalized, and about the same percentage—39 percent in 2024, 37 percent today—think that all undocumented immigrants should be deported. Democrats still have a lot of work to do to regain Latinos’ trust on immigration and the border, and Republicans haven’t suffered nearly as much as one might have expected given the Trump administration’s ruthlessness and cruelty. Latinos are clearly dissatisfied with Trump. The economy was one of his greatest strengths but is now a significant weakness for him. Like all Americans, Latinos say they want the price of food, gas, rent, health care, and other basic needs to be lower. They also want more and better jobs, and higher wages, and for mortgage interest rates to be lower, so they can afford to buy their own home. But they also like Trump’s no-tax-on-tips, overtime-pay, and Social Security policies, and they still generally see Republicans as the pro-business party. An important exception to the almost-exclusive focus on immigration and the economy is the work that Carlos Odio and Rachel Stein, of the Latino research and polling firm Equis , are doing in their newsletter, The New Dynamic . In addition to these issues, they have focused on the Iran war and the strong preference Latinos have for not getting entangled in foreign conflicts more generally, their objection to foreign aid if the trade-off is less investment at home, and the steadfast belief among Latinos, especially more recent arrivals, that the United States is the greatest country in the world. The goal should be not only to “ see with clear eyes what has been revealed in the age of Trump,” as they have written, but also to explore the broad array of issues that shaped Latino life and politics even before Trump entered the arena. For too long, this more expansive approach has been obscured or overshadowed by the issues of immigration and the economy, which can reveal as much about the partisan imperatives of the moment as about Latinos. After last spring’s primaries in Texas, Voto Latino, a Latino voter-mobilization group, asserted that Latinos are “ coming home to Democrats—there is no question about it .” When I mentioned this to Daniel Garza, a longtime Republican and head of the conservative LIBRE Initiative, he said, “There is no home for Latinos.” My hope is that Latinos will claim many political homes instead of just one, and that candidates in all parties continue to fight for votes that we will give them only if they represent the interests of the many communities we are a part of, then follow through on their promises.

items.title: Gao : plusieurs cas de vols et de braquages signalés en moins de 24 heures
items.description: Plusieurs actes de vol et de braquage ont ete signales a Gao entre dimanche soir et lundi 2 novembre. Aux environs du terrain Bahiya, une femme circulant a moto a ete volontairement percutee par deux individus a moto, qui lui ont ensuite arrache son telephone avant de prendre la fuite. Quelques heures plus tot, trois hommes lourdement armes ont braque un jeune derriere le Bloc scientifique, en face de l'hopital regional. Selon la victime, les assaillants l'ont menacee avec leurs armes et ont tente de l'etrangler avec un turban avant de lui soutirer une importante somme d'argent. Dimanche vers 19 heures, un enseignant a egalement ete victime d'un braquage dans le secteur de la Cite Perdue, au quartier Château. Un individu arme lui aurait tire dessus en guise de sommation avant de lui voler sa moto. items.title: Cambriolage à la RTG2 : les équipements du plateau emportés par des individus non identifiés
items.description: Les travailleurs de la Radio Télévision Guinéenne (RTG2) ont été surpris, ce mardi 3 novembre 2026, par le cambriolage de leur régie. Selon nos informations, les malfaiteurs sont passés par la régie avant de briser la baie vitrée pour accéder au grand plateau. Plusieurs équipements, notamment des caméras, ont été emportés. Rencontré sur les lieux, Oumar Touré, connu sous l’appellation « Oumar le Bon », responsable technique de la RTG2, nous a expliqué les circonstances dans lesquelles il a appris la nouvelle. « J’étais à la maison lorsque j’ai été appelé par le responsable du matériel, Sékou Oumar Dabo, qui m’a informé qu’il y avait eu un vol à la RTG. À mon arrivée à la régie, nous avons constaté que la porte avait été forcée. Les individus ont réussi à accéder à l’intérieur et, une fois sur place, ils ont brisé la baie vitrée pour accéder au grand plateau, où ils ont emporté toutes les caméras », a-t-il expliqué. Selon ses explications, au total, 12 équipements ont été emportés par les cambrioleurs. « Les quatre caméras numériques, les micros, notamment les micros HF, au nombre de 12, ont été emportés. Ils ont également pris un mélangeur vidéo, la commande des caméras robotisées ainsi que la mallette. Quant à la console, je crois qu’ils n’ont pas eu le temps de la transporter. Ils l’ont laissée dans le couloir », a-t-il précisé. Pour les travailleurs de la RTG2, il s’agit d’un fait inédit. Oumar Touré explique que, d’habitude, après le journal de 20 heures, les agents mettent en place une programmation destinée à assurer la diffusion des émissions durant toute la nuit. Les clés sont ensuite déposées au poste de gendarmerie situé dans les environs, généralement entre 20 h 30 et 21 heures. « De 21 heures jusqu’au matin, généralement, il n’y a personne sur place. Nous programmons des émissions déjà produites dans la journée pour qu’elles continuent à être diffusées pendant la nuit. Pour le moment, nous ne savons pas exactement comment cela s’est passé », a-t-il indiqué. Au moment où nous mettions cette dépêche en ligne, les services de la gendarmerie étaient déjà présents sur les lieux pour effectuer les premiers constats et ouvrir une enquête afin de faire la lumière sur ce cambriolage. Youl Keita L’article Cambriolage à la RTG2 : les équipements du plateau emportés par des individus non identifiés est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Burkina: en un mois, la Police nationale récolte plus de 99 millions F CFA lors d’une opération
items.description: Dans la matinée du lundi 02 novembre 2026, le Directeur de la Sécurité Publique (DSP), le Commissaire Divisionnaire de Police Sibiri Nébilè Amidou YOIN, a animé un point de presse à la Direction Régionale de la Police Nationale du Kadiogo (DRPN-K). Il était accompagné du Directeur Régional de la Police Nationale du Kadiogo et du Commissaire Central de Police de la ville de Ouagadougou. L'objectif à travers ce point de presse était de faire le bilan à mi-parcours de l'opération « Bouclier Tête durcie » pour la période du 1er au 31 octobre 2026 sur le plan national. Pour le DSP, le bilan est satisfaisant avec un impact positif sur le terrain. Désormais, 98% des usagers des grandes villes, notamment Ouagadougou et Bobo-Dioulasso, et plus de 89% au plan national, respectent la mesure du port obligatoire du casque. Un autre indicateur encourageant est la baisse progressive et significative du nombre d'usagers interpellés pour non respect de la mesure, précisément 14.165 personnes ont été interpellées dans la première semaine d'octobre contre seulement 4518 personnes dans la dernière semaine. Ainsi, pour le mois d'octobre 2026, il ressort des statistiques : 42 448 usagers contrôlés ; 30 424 usagers verbalisés sur place après présentation du casque ; 10 027 engins mis en fourrière pour non-présentation du casque et non paiement de la contravention et 705 engins saisis pour d'autres infractions en matière de circulation routière. La somme totale recouvrée au titre des amendes forfaitaires au profit du Trésor Public s’élève à 99.371.000 FCFA. Le DSP a, au cours du point de presse, rappelé que le port du casque doit cesser d'être perçu comme une simple contrainte réglementaire pour devenir un réflexe de survie. »Le port du casque est un acte révolutionnaire », a-t-il ajouté. Poursuivant, il a traduit la reconnaissance du Camarade Ministre de la Sécurité et du Camarade Directeur Général de la Police Nationale envers les burkinabè qui ont compris la nécessité du port du casque et a invité tous les usagers au port strict du casque. Pour clore, il a annoncé que les équipes déployées sur le terrain vont intensifier les opérations, de jour comme de nuit, pour des résultats plus probants dans le cadre de l'opération « Bouclier Tête Durcie ». La Police Nationale, une force publique au service des citoyens ! L’article Burkina: en un mois, la Police nationale récolte plus de 99 millions F CFA lors d'une opération est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: IHC grants protective bail to TikToker booked following stampede at wedding event
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday granted protective bail to TikToker Muhammad Ansar Jatt, alias “Mr Pattlo”, after a stampede at his mehndi (henna) event in Sialkot claimed two lives. Jatt had announced holding a mehndi event and prize-distribution ceremony at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road on Friday night; however, with hundreds gathered at the site, a stampede occurred when the stadium gates opened, killing two and injuring 18 people. Subsequently, a first information report (FIR) was registered on October 31 at the Motra Police Station, naming Jatt, his brother, the owner of Faraz Cricket Ground, six others, and 40-45 unidentified security guards. On Tuesday, IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar approved the protective — also known as transitory — bail for the TikToker until Nov 10, allowing him to avoid arrest while he approaches the relevant court to seek legal remedy. He surrendered before the court in a wheelchair. Jatt had filed a petition, seeking the court’s intervention to prevent his arrest before he could reach the court of competent jurisdiction. Advocates Barrister Qasim Nawaz Abbasi and Barrister Raja Ali Abbas Jalap filed the petition on his behalf. According to the legal document, Jatt was named in the FIR, which was registered under Sections 322 (punishment for qatl-i-khata ), 440 (mischief committed after preparation made for causing death or hurt), 431 (mischief by injury to public road, bridge, river or channel), 148 (rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 149 (unlawful assembly), 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant) and 109 (punishment of abetment) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), read with Section 16 of the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960. During the proceedings, the petitioner’s counsel argued that the FIR was registered outside the IHC’s territorial jurisdiction. However, the counsel maintained that the sole object of seeking protective bail was to enable a suspect present within the jurisdiction of one court to safely approach the court where the case was registered without being arrested on the way. “The merits of the case are not required to be examined at this stage,” the petition stated, adding that without the protection, the petitioner’s right to seek pre-arrest bail before a Sialkot court would be rendered illusory. The petition further contended that the allegations levelled against the petitioner were “false, frivolous, and baseless,” claiming that he had been falsely implicated. It was also brought to the court’s notice that the petitioner had no previous criminal record and that no other petition seeking the same relief had been filed before any other court. After hearing the arguments, Justice Dogar granted the relief, noting the temporary and limited nature of the protective bail and allowing the petitioner time to surrender before the appropriate forum. On Sunday, Sialkot police said they had arrested six suspects in relation to the incident. Police said Jatt immediately fled the scene after the incident, adding that their investigation and raid teams were conducting operations to apprehend the TikTok influencer. Sialkot District Police Officer Dost Muhammad confirmed that the six arrested individuals were involved in managing the event. According to the DPO, organisers had invited a large number of people by advertising a lucky draw featuring prizes such as motorcycles, a car and other valuable items via social media. During the event, an announcement was made over the loudspeakers instructing all attendees to enter the grounds simultaneously. This simultaneous entry into the sports stadium triggered a severe stampede, the DPO said. He stated that the organisers violated the terms of their permit, as well as established safety standard operating procedures (SOPs). The stampede also disrupted the flow of traffic on the main Daska-Sialkot Road. The Sialkot DPO declared that legal action would be taken against all those responsible for the incident, without any discrimination.

items.title: French judges probe war crimes complaint against Israeli army in Lebanon: lawyer
items.description: France has opened a judicial investigation into a war crimes complaint over an Israeli strike on a residential building in Lebanon, a lawyer told AFP on Tuesday. French-Lebanese artist Ali Cherri, whose parents were killed in the Beirut strike in 2024, filed the complaint as a civil party this year with the International Federation for Human Rights, Cherri’s lawyer Clemence Bectarte explained. The crimes against humanity unit of the Paris Judicial Court has appointed two investigating judges to the case, she added, hailing the move as “a first”. Hezbollah fought with Israel at the start of the war on Gaza following the events of October 7, 2023. The hostilities, which escalated into open war in September 2024, have left more than 4,000 dead in Lebanon and forced more than a million people to flee. Seven civilians, including Cherri’s father and mother, aged 87 and 77, were killed in the bombing of their 12-storey apartment building in central Beirut on November 26, 2024, according to the complaint seen by AFP . Three floors were destroyed. The strike occurred “just a few hours before the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hezbollah came into effect,” the complaint stated, citing detailed research by Amnesty International and Forensic Architecture into the incident. AFP has reached out to the Israeli military for comment. Cherri told AFP he had taken legal action “for the dignity of all civilian victims”. “For nearly two years, I have been fighting… to ensure that the Israeli bombing that killed my parents and five other civilians does not go unpunished,” he said. “What happened to my parents is not an isolated case… I hope this investigation will help break the impunity enjoyed by Israeli officials responsible for attacks against civilians in Lebanon and Palestine,” he added. Several investigations underway While the judicial investigation marks a first over alleged war crimes by Israeli forces in Lebanon, other cases are pending. French-Lebanese man Mohamad H., represented by lawyer Emmanuel Daoud, has sought action after losing his mother, sister, and two nephews in strikes on the southern city of Tyre during the night of April 16-17. In another case, a French entrepreneur born in Lebanon has accused the Israeli army of uprooting 600-century-old olive trees belonging to his family in a village in southern Lebanon. France’s National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT), which handles war crimes, has opened an investigation into allegations of torture and war crimes related to the Israeli forces’ interception of humanitarian flotillas bound for Gaza in 2025 and 2026. The PNAT also asked a Paris judge to open a war crimes investigation into the deaths of two French children in an Israeli bombing in Gaza in October 2023, while ruling out charges of genocide and crimes against humanity, according to sources close to the case.

items.title: Josep Tabernero, oncólogo: “La IA bien aplicada nos va a facilitar las cosas en medicina”
items.description: El mundo está asistiendo a “una revolución” terapéutica y diagnóstica contra el cáncer , ha asegurado el oncólogo Josep Tabernero, director del Vall d’Hebron Institut d’Oncologia (VHIO), durante su intervención en el World in Progress (WIP), el foro internacional organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Barcelona. Cada año se diagnostican 20 millones de nuevos casos de cáncer y eso irá a más, por el envejecimiento y el aumento de la población, pero la supervivencia a esta enfermedad es cada vez mayor: “Cuando empecé la residencia, el 35% de los pacientes sobrevivían al cáncer; ahora estamos cerca del 70%”. Cada vez se conoce más la biología del tumor , hay fármacos más dirigidos, herramientas diagnósticas más precisas y una inteligencia artificial (IA) a disposición de la ciencia de dimensiones impredecibles. “Todavía no llegamos a alcanzar las oportunidades que nos dará . items.title: Orange Burkina Faso: 1 milliard 500 millions de F CFA sur des infrastructures de qualité
items.description: La Fondation Orange Burkina Faso a officialisé, vendredi 30 octobre 2026, une convention de partenariat de 1 milliard 500 millions de F CFA avec l'Initiative présidentielle pour une éducation de qualité (IPEQ). Prévu sur trois ans, cet engagement financier vise la réalisation d'infrastructures éducatives de qualité, dans un contexte où la mobilisation des forces vives est appelée à contribuer à la transformation du système éducatif burkinabè. L'éducation au Burkina Faso peut compter sur un nouvel allié de poids. La Fondation Orange Burkina Faso a décidé de joindre l'acte à l'engagement citoyen, en mobilisant une enveloppe de 1 milliard 500 millions de F CFA au profit de l'Initiative présidentielle pour une éducation de qualité (IPEQ). La convention officialisant cet accompagnement a été signée dans la soirée du vendredi 30 octobre 2026, au cours d'une cérémonie organisée dans les locaux du Bureau national des grands projets du Burkina (BN-GPB), à Ouagadougou. D'un montant global de 1,5 milliard de F CFA, mobilisé sur une période de trois ans, cet engagement financier est destiné à accompagner la réalisation d'infrastructures éducatives de qualité. Une contribution qui entend ainsi prendre part à l'amélioration du cadre d'apprentissage et, au-delà, à la construction d'un système éducatif davantage en mesure de répondre aux aspirations des populations burkinabè. Cérémonie de signature de convention entre la fondation Orange Burkina et L'IPEQ Pour Orange Burkina Faso, cette convention s'inscrit dans une dynamique de mobilisation nationale impulsée par le Chef de l'État, qui a appelé chaque Burkinabè, chaque entreprise, chaque structure et l'ensemble des forces vives à apporter leur contribution au développement du pays. Un appel auquel l'opérateur de téléphonie mobile entend répondre pleinement, en faisant de son engagement citoyen un levier d'action concrète. Loin de se limiter à son cœur de métier, Orange Burkina Faso entend ainsi inscrire son empreinte dans les secteurs stratégiques du développement national, notamment celui de l'éducation. Un choix qui traduit la volonté de l'entreprise de mettre ses capacités et ses ressources au service de causes dont les retombées concernent directement les populations. L'IPEQ rassurée quant à la bonne utilisation des fonds Cette convention entre la fondation Orange Burkina et L'IPEQ matérialise une convergence d'engagements qui de faire de l'éducation le moteur du développement national Du côté de l'Initiative présidentielle pour une éducation de qualité, la signature de cette convention a été accueillie avec satisfaction. Prenant la parole à cette occasion, son coordonnateur, le professeur Zakaria Soré, a exprimé sa reconnaissance à Orange Burkina Faso pour cet accompagnement en faveur du rayonnement du système éducatif national. Il a, notamment, salué un partenariat qui vient renforcer les efforts engagés pour améliorer les conditions d'apprentissage et donner davantage de moyens à l'ambition présidentielle en matière d'éducation. Le coordonnateur de L'IPEQ, le Pr Zakaria Soré « Cet accompagnement de la Fondation Orange Burkina Faso constitue un appui important à notre ambition de bâtir un système éducatif de qualité. Au-delà de la contribution financière, c'est un signal fort de confiance et d'engagement envers l'avenir de notre pays. Nous mesurons pleinement la responsabilité qui accompagne ce soutien et nous veillerons à ce que les ressources mobilisées soient utilisées à bon escient, dans le respect des objectifs fixés et au bénéfice direct de la réussite de l'Initiative présidentielle pour une éducation de qualité», a-t-il fait savoir. Le professeur Zakaria Soré a ainsi rassuré son partenaire quant à la bonne gestion des ressources mises à disposition, avec pour priorité la concrétisation des objectifs assignés au projet. Orange Burkina Faso entend traduire sa responsabilité sociétale en actes Représentant la directrice générale de Orange Burkina Faso, Mme Nafy Silué Coulibaly, le Secrétaire Exécutif de la Fondation, Ibrahim HEMA, a pour sa part replacé cette convention dans le cadre de la responsabilité sociétale de son entreprise. Il a rappelé que l'engagement d'Orange ne se résume pas à connecter les populations à travers ses services de télécommunications, mais consiste également à participer activement à la construction de l'avenir du pays. La directrice générale de Orange Burkina Faso, Mme Nafy Silué Coulibaly apposant sa signature sur la convention de partenariat entre sa structure et L'IPEQ « Notre responsabilité, en tant qu'entreprise citoyenne, ne saurait se limiter à offrir des services de télécommunication et à connecter les populations. Elle nous commande également de prendre notre part dans les grands défis de développement de notre pays. C'est dans cette logique que nous avons choisi d'accompagner l'Initiative présidentielle pour une éducation de qualité, parce que nous sommes convaincus que l'éducation constitue un investissement fondamental pour préparer l'avenir des générations présentes et futures », a souligné Ibrahim HEMA. Pour le représentant de la directrice générale, cet engagement doit surtout se mesurer à l'aune des réalisations concrètes et de leurs retombées sur les populations. La convention signée avec l'IPEQ s'inscrit ainsi dans une vision de la responsabilité sociétale qui privilégie l'action et la contribution effective aux priorités nationales. Ibrahim Hema, Secrétaire exécutif de la fondation Orange Burkina « À travers cette convention de 1 milliard 500 million de F CFA sur trois ans, nous voulons apporter une contribution tangible à l'amélioration des infrastructures éducatives au Burkina Faso. Il ne s'agit pas simplement d'annoncer un engagement financier, mais de participer à une dynamique qui doit produire des résultats concrets et durables. Nous voulons que notre action contribue à offrir aux apprenants de meilleures conditions d'éducation, car investir dans des infrastructures de qualité, c'est aussi investir dans les compétences, les opportunités et le devenir de toute une nation », a-t-il ajouté. Photo de famille Au-delà de la signature protocolaire, cette convention entre la Fondation Orange Burkina Faso et l'IPEQ matérialise ainsi une convergence d'engagements autour d'un enjeu majeur qui est de faire de l'éducation un véritable moteur du développement national. Avec 1,5 milliard de F CFA annoncés sur trois ans, la Fondation Orange Burkina Faso inscrit sa contribution dans la durée et entend faire de sa responsabilité sociétale un engagement au service des priorités du Burkina Faso. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Orange Burkina Faso: 1 milliard 500 millions de F CFA sur des infrastructures de qualité est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: L’Europe se dirige-t-elle vers une nouvelle crise énergétique cet hiver ?
items.description: Le vortex polaire stratosphérique, une vaste circulation hivernale qui s’étend au-dessus de chaque pôle, s’effondre généralement à la fin du mois de janvier. Cette année, plusieurs modèles météorologiques indiquent qu’il pourrait s’effondrer dès les prochains jours, ce qui en ferait l’effondrement le plus précoce jamais enregistré et serait susceptible d’entraîner, dans les semaines suivantes, un afflux d’air arctique vers l’Amérique du Nord et l’Europe Record-Early Polar Vortex Collapse Puts Energy Traders on Alert », Bloomberg , 2 novembre 2026.'> 1 . Une vague de froid précoce pèserait sur les stocks européens de gaz naturel, qui se trouvent à leur niveau le plus faible à ce moment de l’année depuis le début des relevés de Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), en 2011. Les capacités de stockage de l’Union n’étaient remplies qu’à 74,6 % au 1er novembre, contre 82,8 % l’an dernier et 95,2 % en 2024. Dans un rapport publié aujourd’hui, mardi 3 novembre, l’Agence internationale de l’énergie estime que des températures hivernales plus froides que la normale en Europe, combinées à une fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz jusqu’à fin mars, pourraient augmenter la consommation de gaz dans les bâtiments de plus de 10 %, et de 7 % dans le secteur de l’électricité entre novembre et mars, par rapport à l’hiver dernier Global Gas Security Review 2026 , Agence internationale de l'énergie, 3 novembre 2026.'> 2 . Dans l’industrie, les prix élevés conduiraient à un recul de 15 % de la consommation, soit une destruction de la demande similaire à celle de la crise énergétique de 2022-2023, après l’invasion russe de l’Ukraine. Le prix du mégawattheure de gaz avait alors dépassé 330 euros en août 2022, soit plus de 1 000 % de plus qu’un an plus tôt. Dans son scénario le plus défavorable, l’AIE estime que les stocks européens de gaz pourraient tomber en dessous de 10 % de leur capacité dès début mars 2027, et finir l’hiver à 7 %. Il s’agirait de leur niveau le plus faible jamais enregistré – même en mars 2022, leur niveau n’était pas passé sous les 25 %. À un tel niveau, les capacités de soutirage des sites de stockage souterrain seraient réduites en raison de la baisse de pression dans les réservoirs. Une vague de froid tardive, associée notamment à une faible production d’énergie éolienne, pourrait alors accroître le risque de volatilité des prix et de ruptures d’approvisionnement, ce qui pèserait sur les industries et les budgets des ménages. L’article L’Europe se dirige-t-elle vers une nouvelle crise énergétique cet hiver ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Nécrologie : le journaliste Lanciné Camara du quotidien national HOROYA est décédé à Bamako
items.description: Le monde de la presse guinéenne est en deuil. Le journaliste Lanciné Camara, du quotidien national HOROYA, est décédé ce mardi à Bamako, en République du Mali. La disparition de ce professionnel des médias constitue une triste nouvelle pour l’ensemble de la corporation journalistique guinéenne. Journaliste et ancien secrétaire général de rédaction au sein du quotidien national HOROYA, Lanciné Camara laisse derrière lui une famille, des confrères et des proches plongés dans la tristesse. Travailleur assidu et sociable, celui que beaucoup appelaient affectueusement « doyen » avait consacré l’essentiel de sa vie professionnelle au métier de journaliste, notamment au sein du journal HOROYA. Apprécié pour ses qualités humaines et son engagement professionnel, il laisse le souvenir d’un confrère dévoué à son métier. items.title: Rencontre à Djerba des anesthésistes-réanimateurs pédiatriques francophones
items.description: L’île de Djerba accueillera, les 12 et 13 novembre 2026, les premières Journées francophones d’anesthésie-réanimation pédiatriques, organisées conjointement par la Société tunisienne d’anesthésie, d’analgésie et de réanimation ( Staar ) et l’Association des anesthésistes-réanimateurs pédiatriques d’expression française (Adarpef). Cet événement scientifique international réunira des médecins spécialistes, des professeurs universitaires et des experts tunisiens, français et internationaux autour des dernières avancées en anesthésie-réanimation pédiatrique. Au programme : conférences scientifiques, ateliers de formation, échanges d’expertise et présentations des innovations visant à améliorer la qualité et la sécurité de la prise en charge anesthésique des enfants. Au-delà de sa dimension scientifique, ce congrès constitue un symbole fort de la coopération médicale franco-tunisienne, favorisant le partage des connaissances entre les deux rives de la Méditerranée et contribuant au rayonnement scientifique et médical de la Tunisie à l’international. Cette manifestation s’adresse aux médecins anesthésistes-réanimateurs, pédiatres, techniciens d’anesthésie et à l’ensemble des professionnels de santé concernés par la prise en charge pédiatrique. items.title: IHC suspends order rejecting FIR plea in Pims fire case, seeks inquiry report and govt response
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday suspended a Justice of the Peace’s order dismissing an application seeking the registration of an FIR into the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) neonatal fire tragedy . The court also directed the authorities to submit the complete record, along with the inquiry report, and issued notices to the respondents, including the federal government and the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). The August 26 fire at a nursery in Pims’ Mother and Child Hospital claimed the lives of 14 newborns. The incident raised concerns over fire safety measures and sparked calls for accountability , with criminal action being ordered against eight officials . “I will call for all reports and summon all evidence,” Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro observed while hearing a petition filed by lawyer Riaz Hanif Rahi on behalf of The Jurists Foundation of Pakistan. “If any negligence comes to light, I will order the registration of a case against those responsible,” the judge added. The petition seeks the registration of an FIR in connection with the deaths of 14 newborns in a fire at the Gynaecology Ward/Special Care Centre of the Mother and Child Hospital (MCH) at Pims. The petitioner alleged that the incident was caused by gross negligence, including the absence of staff from a ward that had reportedly been locked to prevent theft. Earlier, on Aug 28, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered an inquiry against eight Pims officials over alleged negligence in addressing fire-safety deficiencies. The report alleged that the officials failed to take timely corrective measures despite being alerted to safety shortcomings, and that the subsequent tragedy could have been prevented. “In the Pims tragedy, 14 children were burned simultaneously,” he said, adding that “even among wild animals in the jungle, such a thing does not happen,” said the counsel. Justice Soomro, however, asked the counsel to restrict his submissions to the legal aspects of the case. When Rahi continued narrating details of the tragedy, the judge remarked: “You are veering off track again; please present legal arguments pertaining to your case.” The counsel argued that no FIR had been registered in the deaths to date. The judge asked whether an inquiry had been conducted. Rahi replied that the inquiry report had established negligence and urged the court to direct the registration of an FIR before the end of the court’s working hours. Explaining the delay, the counsel said the Justice of the Peace had dismissed his application on the grounds that petitions relating to the matter were already pending before the high court. He argued that, apart from him, no one else had approached the police station seeking the registration of a case and that an FIR should have been registered. “I have gathered so much evidence — but if an FIR is not registered, where am I supposed to take this evidence?” he asked. After hearing the arguments, the court suspended the Justice of the Peace’s order and directed the authorities to submit the complete record, including the inquiry reports, before the next hearing. It also directed that all evidence be placed on record. Other prayers The petition, filed under Article 199 of the Constitution, also seeks directions for the respondents to compensate the victims’ families under Section 323 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). It further asks the court to restrain government medical staff, including doctors, from engaging in private practice, particularly at commercial establishments, unless permitted under a validly framed law. Among other reliefs sought, the petitioner has asked the court to direct the Islamabad Healthcare Regulatory Authority to include individuals such as Dr Khaliq-uz-Zaman in its governing body, ensure that the relevant institutions meet ISO standards and direct the Auditor General to submit audit reports. In the event of any discrepancies, the petition seeks directions for the FIA to initiate proceedings. The petition also calls for the replacement of expired electrical wiring in government hospitals. It further seeks a declaration that placing newborns in isolation is unreasonable, illogical and illegal, and runs counter to maternal love. It further asks the court to declare the construction of the Mother and Child Hospital an encroachment on the hospital’s already approved plan and direct that the neonatal units be reconfigured so newborns can be placed within sight of their mothers and close to their beds. The petitioner has also sought compensatory costs for filing the public interest litigation. The court issued notices to the federal government through the Cabinet secretary, the Prime Minister’s Office, the Ministry of Interior, the Establishment Division, the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council, the Islamabad Healthcare Regulatory Authority, the Auditor General of Pakistan, the Islamabad chief commissioner and deputy commissioner, the Capital Development Authority, Capital Emergency Services, the executive director of Pims, the Islamabad inspector general of police, the SSP Operations, the FIA director general and other respondents, seeking their replies. The hearing was adjourned until Nov 12.

items.title: Petitions against detention of Sohail Afridi, others referred to PHC CJ for constitution of larger bench
items.description: PESHAWAR: A Peshawar High Court (PHC) bench on Tuesday referred multiple petitions challenging the detention of PTI leaders, including Sohail Afridi — the non-functional Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister — to the chief justice for the constitution of a larger bench. Afridi has not been seen since the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11. His whereabouts remained unknown on the day governor’s rule was imposed, and a federal minister confirmed a day later that he and some of his cabinet members were in preventive custody . The PTI has also alleged the detention and arrests of several of its other members, including lawmakers and ministers. Their whereabouts have not been disclosed by the government so far. Multiple pleas have been filed in the PHC in this connection. A division bench comprising Justice Syed Arshad Ali and Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali took up the petitions on Tuesday. Apart from Afridi’s detention, the petitions also pertain to the alleged disappearance of KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, MNAs Junaid Akbar and Dr Amjid Ali, provincial minister Amjid Ali Khan, MPAs Ikramullah and Aurangzeb Khan, former chief minister of Gilgit-Baltistan Mohammad Khalid Khursheed and several other PTI leaders. Afridi’s brother Mohammad Aamir filed one of the petitions, alleging that Afridi was “abducted” from Chief Minister House on the night that the emergency was imposed in the province. He had approached the PHC on Oct 13. On Tuesday, the bench referred the pleas to the chief justice after the KP government and senior police officials failed to file their respective replies in accordance with the court’s Oct 20 directives . “These are not ordinary personalities,” remarked Justice Ali during the hearing. Meanwhile, KP Advocate General Sanaullah Khan sought three days to submit the replies, adding that his office was awaiting a response from the provincial home department, police and other law enforcement agencies. Bashir Vazir, who appeared on behalf of the petitioners, alleged that the PTI leaders had been missing for many days. He contended that, under Article 199 of the Constitution, the PHC had authority to order that Afridi and Swati be produced before the court. He further argued that the KP Assembly had passed an immunity law under which a member of the assembly could not be arrested in such manner, adding that the assembly’s speaker also could not be arrested under the law. The law stipulated that the speaker would remain in office until a successor is elected, Vazir said. According to the KP advocate general, in more than 200 instances of detentions under the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO), orders were passed without the cases being heard. The bench disagreed with the claim, observing that in those cases reports had been sought from the respondents but were never submitted. It further observed that the detentions under consideration were not MPO cases. “This is an important case; the chief minister of the province is missing,” Justice Ali observed. The bench said the court had given the respondents 10 days to file replies, but they had not complied with the order. “We refer this case to the chief justice to constitute a larger bench,” Justice Ali said. The KP advocate general also requested the constitution of a larger bench.

items.title: Israel’s Common Ground
items.description: My most recent visit to Israel overlapped with its election in October, but that was a coincidence. In 10 days of discussions with generals and intelligence officers, entrepreneurs and university students, I was reminded of what Moshe Dayan’s biographer Shabtai Teveth wrote about Israel’s famous one-eyed soldier and diplomat: “His one eye glimmered with an enormous lust for life, his other eye was extinguished beneath the black patch, dead. At times he seemed to symbolize Israel itself, in which life and death are close partners.” I had visited Israel in November 2023, while the horrors of the Hamas onslaught were still fresh—more than 800 civilians and 300 soldiers killed, 251 hostages seized. I saw the room where one disabled old woman had been burned alive in bed; the house where a father was killed in front of his children, the scattered toys and playthings. Only the bloodstains had, in accordance with Jewish ritual, been painstakingly removed. It was a country in deep and open trauma. The trauma is no longer on the surface. The traffic jams are back, the restaurants are reasonably full, and the collective settlements along the Gaza envelope are being rebuilt by those who’d fled them, along with new volunteers. The trauma, however, is now like an artesian river: running below the surface, but immensely powerful. The election offered proof of that. Although important substantive issues were at stake—efforts to restrict the independence of the judicial system, or the question of universal national service, for example—the election was about personalities: whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was to be loathed or trusted; whether the ultraright leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would retain a place in government; whether Israel should trust Gadi Eisenkot, an admired and respected retired general but a political novice, who had lost a son and two nephews in the fighting. [ View: Flying across the world to vote ] Foreign and national-security policy were not major concerns. Israelis are far harder than they were more than three years ago. Those who believe that a two-state solution is achievable in the near term, rather than a modus vivendi with the Palestinians, are found only on the political margins. The aggressive establishment of buffer zones in Gaza and Lebanon—roughly 10 kilometers of devastation in southern Lebanon, as the civilian population is pushed out—receives general approval. Such restraint in the use of force as most Israelis favor is based on the narrowest considerations of prudence rather than on foreign opinion. Israelis do not give a damn about criticism from European leaders, or feeble and performative gestures, such as their recognition of a Palestinian state whose rulers have not called an election in two decades. Israelis ignore foreign politicians who make statements and proclamations but do not bother to visit their country. Young Israelis compete to get into elite units in the Israel Defense Forces; when a war breaks out, the planes coming home are jammed with Israelis returning to serve in the IDF, while the ones leaving carry mainly foreigners. Thus, Israelis have little use for students in distant lands who are innocent of the experience of war, wearing keffiyehs and blocking campuses. They despise those who call their campaign in Gaza—which was indeed ferocious—genocide. Nearly 500 members of the IDF have been killed in Gaza since October 8, 2023, and many thousands more wounded. Israelis know that humanitarian aid has been flowing into Gaza through their territory; that Gaza’s population has actually grown over the past 10 years; and that Hamas, although no longer possessing an army of 25,000 well-equipped infantry exploiting the biggest military tunnel network in history, is still in charge in Gaza, still fighting, and still clinging to its ultimate goal of destroying their state. In many ways, Israelis have turned inward, and the results may be dangerous for them. They do not pay a great deal of heed, for example, to the waves of anti-Semitic rhetoric and criminal attacks that have swept countries where they would once have been unthinkable, such as Britain and the United States. To the extent that they do, they merely see it as confirmation of their belief that the world’s oldest hate is at work, rather than a reaction to anything they’ve done. Worse, this grim view leads many of them, including military and political leaders, to give up on public diplomacy as hopeless. They do not understand how much the thuggery of some West Bank settlers brutalizing local Palestinians has damaged their country’s standing. They do not fully appreciate the significance of the collapse of support in both American political parties, or the alienation of some of their previously committed supporters in the Jewish and evangelical-Christian communities. “The whole world is against us,” once the refrain of a mocking song from the past century, seems to them a given. Proud, possibly overly proud, of their deepening relationships with some parts of the Arab world and with states such as India, they run the risk of losing their most valuable security and trading partners in Europe and the United States. They see renewed bouts of battle approaching. On the Lebanon border, in particular, Hezbollah has reconstituted and begun rearming. But although it had planned, before 2023, an assault along the border similar to but on a larger scale than that of October 7, it is shifting its approach. The drone wars of Ukraine and the Persian Gulf are coming to Israel, with fiber-optic-guided drones that render the new buffer zone less relevant. Israelis know that Iran is still waiting for its opportunity, and has new weapons that can pierce their country’s sophisticated, but nonetheless limited, defenses. Thus far the black eye patch. But there is another side as well. Israel’s economy has, astonishingly, continued to grow at 4 percent annually. Many Israelis—not just the ultra-Orthodox—continue to have families of three or more children, a stark contrast to the birth dearth of advanced societies in Europe and Asia. Israel ranks eighth in the world happiness index , just behind Norway but ahead of Switzerland, Ireland, and Canada. Israel may be a start-up nation, but the key to its strength is social cohesion. An American businessman I asked about the difference in organizational culture noted with a grin that in the New York financial world, where he had worked, employees ate at their desk. Here, his company gives chits to workers so that they can go out together for a proper lunch. Extended families, secular as well as religious, gather for Friday-night dinners. When I waited with a colleague at a road junction near the Lebanese border to meet another friend, every car that passed—without exception—stopped and asked if we needed help. [ Graeme Wood: Israel can’t postpone its reckoning forever ] My trip began with a visit to Reichman University, Israel’s only private university. Uriel Reichman, its founder, is a former dean of Tel Aviv University law school who hated Israel’s stodgy higher-education bureaucracy. He created, over 30 years, a spectacular campus with state-of-the-art studios, classrooms, and laboratories. Reichman, now the president emeritus, is hard at work building a medical school. His modest office, and that of the current president, sits in a small, spartan one-story building on the gleaming campus. By design, he and his successor bump into students and faculty, and they into them. There are nice cafeterias on campus, but no faculty club. My visit coincided with a memorial ceremony for Yitzhak Rabin, the prime minister assassinated in 1995, who had been the victorious chief of staff during the 1967 Six-Day War. The lanky provost, a lawyer whose expertise lies in mergers and acquisitions, gave a powerful speech to the assembled students, a cheerful and fit-looking lot, even those with missing limbs from their military service. Nearby stood memorials to their fallen fellows, including one who had been taken hostage in Gaza. He quoted Rabin’s speech given barely two weeks after the Six-Day War, while receiving an honorary doctorate from Hebrew University. The victories had been spectacular; Rabin’s tone, however, was somber. He’d asked: What is there in common between military activity and the academic world which represents civilization and culture? What is there in common between those whose profession is violence, and spiritual values? For Rabin, the answer lay in “the unique spirit of the entire Jewish people.” He’d continued: We find, increasingly, a strange phenomenon among our fighters. Their joy is not total, and more than a little sorrow, and shock, permeates their celebration. There are those who do not celebrate at all. The warriors in the front lines witnessed not only the glory of victory but also its price—their comrades who fell beside them, bleeding. And I know that the terrible price paid by our enemies also touched the hearts of many of our men deeply. It may be that the Jewish people never learned, never accustomed themselves to experience the thrill of conquest and victory, and so we receive it with mixed feelings. Hovering over the Israelis of 1967 were the horrors of the Holocaust. Today the living memories of those events are almost gone. New demons, however, haunt an Israel that has lived through more history—some of it sordid, some of it horrible—since Rabin gave his speech. The country has more things to be ashamed of, and a greater amount of things to be proud of. But surprisingly, beneath it lies, including in the living spirit of Rabin’s sober speech, more solid common ground than one might think.

items.title: The Voters Sitting This One Out
items.description: O ver the past decade, Andrew Leyva shaded the space next to Donald Trump’s name each time it appeared on his ballot, trusting that a tough-talking businessman willing to challenge Washington would benefit working guys like him. Leyva, a 39-year-old who installs blinds in Arizona, voted to usher in the economic “golden age” that Trump so often promised. Leyva envisioned gas that cost $2 a gallon. Government spending would be cut. The influence of the wealthy and well-connected would be minimized. Regular people would finally get their say, and America would always come first. It didn’t take long after Trump’s second win for Leyva to realize that he had been duped. First, he said, Trump seemed to obstruct the release of the Epstein files, which didn’t live up to the MAGA-sphere hype when some of them were finally made public. Then the president did something he had said he wasn’t going to do: start a war. Leyva now spends nearly twice as much on gas as he did last year—sometimes it costs him $300 a week. I ran into him outside a home-improvement store in Scottsdale, where voters will decide one of the nation’s competitive congressional races. I asked whether he was planning to vote. “Hell no. I don’t think it matters,” he told me as he loaded blinds into his gleaming Toyota pickup. Trump was supposed to be different, Leyva said, but it turns out that he’s just as bad as every other politician. Leyva doesn’t think that he’ll ever vote again. I’d grown accustomed to this sort of response, given the many people who have told me over the past year about their deep distrust of America’s political system. They have no confidence in major parties or the voting process, and they believe that some sort of fix is already in. Their votes won’t make a difference, many told me, so why bother casting a ballot? For some, Trump was their last hope. They hadn’t typically voted, but they made an exception in his case. When he failed to live up to his promises, any expectation that voting could solve their problems evaporated. The Trump era has brought with it a paradox: Even as Americans say that they find politics to be more toxic than ever, more of them are participating; the 2020 election had the most voters in history, and more than 158 million ballots were cast. Republican nonvoters have been galvanized by Trump, and voters who oppose him have engaged with politics for the first time. But one of the central questions of the midterms is whether Americans will continue this level of involvement. Those who, like Leyva, decide to sit out today’s election could help determine the balance of power in Congress. In close contests, the people who don’t show up matter as much as the people who do: Even small shifts in turnout can determine winners and losers, especially in tight races and swing states. Parties, candidates, and outside groups have spent months trying to motivate people to show up. It can be easier to persuade a reluctant voter to cast a ballot than it is to change the mind of a consistent one who is committed to a party. But in an election defined by anger over soaring gas and grocery prices, this could prove difficult—particularly for GOP campaigns seeking to motivate people who turned out for Trump and now regret showing up at all. [ Read: Going hungry in Trump’s economy ] The grim mood has left Republicans battling to defend themselves, not just in swing seats but also in what was overwhelmingly friendly territory two years ago. Nonvoters and occasional voters are vital to the prospects of both parties. But all year, I have spoken with Americans who said that they no longer see the point. Some requested anonymity to talk candidly, saying they didn’t want employers or family members to read about their true feelings. One young Republican couple who were wrestling two fussy toddlers into their car seats told me that they cast their ballots for Trump in 2024, hoping he would make it easier for them to buy a home in Arizona. Now home prices are out of reach, and consistently high interest rates have made borrowing too expensive. They’re moving to El Paso, Texas, where the husband has accepted a job on the police force. They aren’t voting, because they’re too busy getting ready for the move. The problem doesn’t afflict just Republicans. Some voters who cast ballots for Democrats in 2024 are also unwilling to make the effort again. A 40-year-old woman who supported Kamala Harris told me that she now doubts her place in the political process. The parties know that she took part in the previous election, and they’re banging on her door, seeking an encore. She doesn’t want to talk with them, because nothing they could say would persuade her to vote: “I look pretty young,” she said, “so I tell them my parents aren’t home.” She and others I spoke with said that they’re so burned-out by the constant controversies involving Trump and his administration that they’ve stopped paying attention. Some said they now go out of their way to avoid news coverage about the president. When they accidentally stumble on it, they’re unsure whom to believe and move on to more entertaining content to avoid growing anxious or overwhelmed. None of the people I talked with believed that the president, the federal government, or either political party were improving their lives. Many said that they trust only the officials they can see in their communities, such as city-council members and police. A lack of confidence in the electoral system also helps explain the lack of motivation. Trump’s obsession with falsely claiming that the 2020 election was stolen from him has damaged faith that votes will be accurately tallied. Many people I talked with repeated his unproven claims about election equipment flipping votes and foreign conspiracies undermining the will of the American voter. One man told me he didn’t think voting was worth the hassle of tracking down documents that prove his citizenship—something Trump wants to make mandatory but that is not yet required to cast a ballot. Making an effort is pointless when no one is listening and political promises are made to be broken, these voters said. “Our United States,” Leyva said, “has just been failing us.” R onald, who was heading into a Phoenix gym after work last month, doesn’t really identify with a political party. He’s fiscally conservative and socially liberal and has voted for both Democrats and Republicans. He didn’t like Kamala Harris in 2024 but cast a ballot for her anyway. Ronald, who didn’t want his full name used, because he doesn’t want his friends and family to know his true political feelings, is appalled by the ballooning national debt and worries that a financial crisis is on the horizon. He told me that he’s tired of candidates who seem consumed with tearing each other down at the expense of actual issues. He can’t escape campaign advertisements accusing candidates of protecting sexual predators. As he was telling me this, Ronald formed his hand into a circle and held it up to his mouth, pretending it was a microphone. “This guy fucking loves pedophiles!” he yelled, mocking political ads playing nonstop across Arizona, where candidates for governor are accusing one another of being soft on child abuse. Ronald used to vote regularly. But the ads and their “dramatization of politics” are a major reason he decided not to bother this year. “I’m so fed up,” he said. He wants to provide value to society through his personal life and is leaving making the right political call to the people who participate today. “I just want to be a good person,” he said, “and I’ll see you all next time.” In the past decade, 41 percent of eligible voters participated in all three presidential elections, according to the Pew Research Center, and one-quarter didn’t vote in any of the contests. When compared with people who did participate, the people who didn’t were younger, had lower family incomes, and were less likely to be white or to have gone to college, the study found. In 2024, Trump aggressively targeted nonvoters, and it worked: Among people who hadn’t voted in the previous two presidential contests, he carried the group by 55 percent, compared with Harris’s 41 percent. A major question looming over today’s vote is whether those people show up again—and if so, whether they will stick with Republicans. Lorna Romero Ferguson, a Republican political consultant in Arizona, told me that voter apathy reflects a fundamental unhappiness with the government and political leaders. “When you lose people who are either die-hard Democrats or die-hard Republicans that you typically could count on,” she said, “then it becomes a crapshoot on Election Day.” Between the conspiracies and the burn-it-to-the-ground style that have come to define today’s politics, both parties are making regular people feel uninspired. “It’s hard to really motivate an electorate that’s so upset and so turned off by politics,” Romero Ferguson said. [ Read: Trump has pushed some Texas Republicans too far ] Jamie Garcia, who recently moved to Phoenix from El Paso for a job as an X-ray tech, teared up when I asked why she doesn’t regularly vote. No one in her family ever talked about politics or voting, she told me, even though her dad, a Mexican immigrant, was able to become a citizen after President Ronald Reagan signed an act that gave undocumented people a path to citizenship. She voted for the first and only time in 2020, amid pandemic-era restrictions. She cast her ballot for Joe Biden, thinking he would improve the nation’s health-care system. She hasn’t shown up again. The news stresses her out because she doesn’t know who is telling the truth or how to even begin to decipher fact from fiction. She has thought about asking friends for advice about how to start becoming politically engaged, but she’s afraid that people will judge her for not having paid attention. She haltingly asked me for help: “How can I be educated more, as far as governors and stuff like that, or just what’s going on in my city—even starting with that—without feeling so overwhelmed or so stressed?” Both parties must now try to break through to voters like Garcia, the ones who have deliberately turned away.
